Commentary.Commentary: We are back! The two umpires make their way out to the middle. Suryakumar Yadav leads his troops out to the middle. Saim Ayub and Sahibzada Farhan will open the innings for Pakistan. Hardik Pandya will start with the new ball. Hardik to Farhan with a slip in place. Here we go!
... THE RUN CHASE ....

Looking ahead - The tacky nature of the surface has clearly favoured the slower bowlers. India have gone with an extra spinner in Kuldeep Yadav tonight, and the likes of Tilak Varma and Abhishek Sharma can also chip in with the ball. Pakistan will aim to make the Powerplay count. Once the ball softens, stroke-making could become far more challenging on this surface. Please stay tuned for the run chase.

Pakistan's fightback - Pakistan fought their way back into the contest after removing Ishan and managed to keep the scoring in check through their spinners. Abrar Ahmed went for plenty on the night and could not quite make the conditions count, but Saim Ayub delivered an excellent spell, finishing with figures of 3 for 25 from his four overs. There was plenty of talk about how India would fare against Usman Tariq, and they handled him reasonably well.

Ishan's onslaught after early jolt - Salman Agha pulled off a surprise first up and it worked perfectly, dismissing Abhishek in his opening over. Pakistan, however, failed to build on that early breakthrough as Ishan Kishan made them pay for anything loose. He continued to dominate even after the Powerplay, with Tilak Varma largely playing second fiddle in their stand. Ishan scored 76 of the 87 runs in that partnership, and at one stage, India were cruising at 10 an over with 82 on the board at the end of 8 overs.

A magnificent batting effort! End of the Indian innings, one that ebbed and flowed. Given how the pitch has behaved, India will take 175. Pakistan, though, will have mixed feelings. With the way Ishan Kishan was going, India looked destined for a bigger total. Pakistan did well to pull things back through the middle overs, but at the death, with Shaheen Afridi not quite nailing the final over, they were unable to prevent India from crossing 170.

OUT! CAUGHT! Not the best of balls by Shaheen, as this is full and outside off, with a slight pace taken off. Axar Patel swings across to slog it over deep mid-wicket, but his bat turns at the point of contact and goes only as far as deep mid-wicket. Saim Ayub runs in off the ropes and tumbles across to his left to pluck the catch. INDIA FINISH AT 175/7, with 16 runs coming from the final over.

Commentary.Commentary: DRINKS BREAK. It is delicately poised at the moment. India have scored 73/1 after the Powerplay. But Pakistan have not allowed these two to free their arms. Still, SKY and Tilak have played the situation nicely in this middle phase and have kept the scorecard churning with ones and twos. Looking at how the pitch has played so far and with 8 wickets in hand, and a lot of arm and ammunition left in the order, one of these two will look to put the foot on the accelerator now. Pakistan, meanwhile, will need to break this partnership as quickly as possible to stall the run rate. Saim Ayub (3-0-23-1) is back on.

Commentary.Commentary: DRINKS BREAK! India will be relatively happy with the start. Despite losing Abhishek Sharma in the very first over, they have managed to keep the scoreboard ticking at close to 9 runs an over. The tacky nature of the surface has been evident in the opening exchanges, but Pakistan have not quite been able to string together consistent pressure with the ball. It remains to be seen how the middle phase unfolds as the ball begins to soften, and whether Pakistan can improve their discipline and make the conditions count.

FOUR! Good effort in the deep, but goes in vain. Tossed up, full and around leg at 84.9 kph. It lands, grips slightly and turns away. Varma shuffles outside leg, stretches forward and looks to push it away from his body, but gets a faint outside edge. The ball trickles along the ground, sneaking through between the keeper and short third. The sub fielder, Khawaja Nafay, from short third sprints after it and tries to flick it back in play with a dive, but he does not do so cleanly. The replay shows that his body was in contact with the ropes while holding the ball in his hand. India end their Powerplay with 52/1 on the board. This also brings up the 50-run partnership between Ishan and Tilak.

Commentary.Commentary: The anthems are sung/chanted with pride and it is time to get down to real business in the Sri Lankan capital. The stands are packed to the rafters with not a single vacant seat. The two umpires walk out as the Pakistani players form a last-minute huddle before spreading across the park. Now then, the two Indian openers - Abhishek Sharma and Ishan Kishan make their way out to the crease. And we will have spin straightaway. The Pakistani skipper, Salman Agha, has the new ball. Two left-handers at the crease. Interesting stuff. Ishan to face. Here we go!

National anthem time - A great sight as the giant flags of both countries are unveiled in the middle. Out come the match officials. And now, the players of both teams walk out through the fireworks along with the mascots as it is time for the national anthems. It will be Pakistan's first, followed by the Indian national anthem.

PITCH REPORT - Harbhajan Singh and Parthiv Patel are pitchside. Harbhajan shares that the surface looks well-rolled and hard, adding that it is the same pitch where Zimbabwe had defeated Australia a few days ago, albeit in a day game. He explains that with this being a night fixture and the pitch having been rolled nicely, it should offer good batting conditions with plenty of runs on offer. Bhajji expects the surface to slow down with time. He also points out that the bigger boundaries would make clearing the ropes more challenging. Parthiv then details the ground dimensions, stating that the square boundaries are 74 metres and 70 metres. He adds that the straight boundary is the longest at 84 metres, stressing that big hitting would require precise execution. Harbhajan adds that the team capable of rotating strike effectively, mixing singles and doubles with occasional boundaries, would hold the advantage. He feels that the pitch would not offer much spin, making adaptability crucial, especially given the large dimensions. He highlights that players who handle spin well and play intelligently would have the upper hand. For the seamers, he advises bowling back of a length and relying on cutters to be effective on this surface.

The Indian skipper - Suryakumar Yadav says that they were looking to bat first. Shares that they have seen the past results here and that they have won the previous two games while batting first, so they don't want to change anything. He admits it is easy to say it is just another game, but acknowledges that it is an occasion with high stakes. Believes that it is important to stay in the present and be clear about what you want to do. Adds that sport teaches you many lessons, and on any given day, anyone can step up and make a difference. Informs that Abhishek Sharma is back and Kuldeep Yadav comes in for Arshdeep Singh.

The captain of Pakistan - Salman Agha says it looks like a tacky wicket, so he feels that it will assist the bowlers for the first few overs and adds that they want to use that. Mentions that they are relaxed and focused in the group and excited for this challenge. About the observations from the previous game here, he says it is a bigger ground than the SSC and details that it is a bit slower too. Shares that they have been playing on these kinds of pitches for the last few months, so they have the idea about how to play in such conditions. Informs that they are going with the same side for this game.
Pakistan (Unchanged Playing XI) - Saim Ayub, Sahibzada Farhan, Salman Agha (C), Babar Azam, Usman Khan (WK), Shadab Khan, Mohammad Nawaz, Faheem Ashraf, Shaheen Afridi, Abrar Ahmed and Usman Tariq.

India (Playing XI) - Abhishek Sharma (In for Sanju Samson), Ishan Kishan (WK), Tilak Varma, Suryakumar Yadav (C), Hardik Pandya, Shivam Dube, Rinku Singh, Axar Patel, Kuldeep Yadav (In for Arshdeep Singh), Varun Chakaravarthy and Jasprit Bumrah.

TOSS - Time for the coin to go up in Colombo. Suryakumar Yadav and Salman Agha have made their way out to the middle. 'Heads' is the call from Salman, and he gets it right. Pakistan elect to BOWL first.

Namibia out of reckoning - Gerhard Erasmus's side has suffered their third straight defeat, going down to the USA in the afternoon game in Chennai. The Monank Patel-led USA posted 199, and although Namibia looked promising at the halfway mark of the chase, they eventually lost momentum and fell away. The USA remain in the race, while the winner tonight here in Colombo will qualify for the Super 8 stage.

Look who's here - Former India captain Rohit Sharma, the man who led the team to their last T20 World Cup triumph, is in the house. Rohit, who is also an ambassador for this World Cup, is seen on the sidelines greeting the Indian players as they prepare for the big clash.

Time for the action - Enough of the numbers. It is time to get down to business. Strap in, because this promises to be a contest worthy of all the hype. As for the weather in Colombo, conditions are currently dry and let's hope it stays that way. With the weather holding up, it has allowed Indian rapper Hanumankind to get the atmosphere buzzing ahead of this blockbuster clash.

Batting might, bowling bite - With the bat, the firepower is undeniable. Since the last T20 World Cup, India, with 388 sixes and Pakistan, with 316, rank among the top three for most sixes hit in T20Is among the teams present at this World Cup. Their bowling numbers are equally striking. Among the teams competing at this World Cup, these two are part of an elite trio averaging under 20 with the ball in T20Is during this period, with India at 18.6 and Pakistan close behind at 19.4.

Subcontinental stronghold - Sri Lankan conditions have proven fruitful for both sides. They are the only visiting teams with more than 10 T20I wins in the country, with India winning 15 of their 19 matches and Pakistan claiming 11 wins from 15 outings.

Beyond the head-to-head - The head-to-head record in T20 World Cups may read 7-1 in India's favour, and the Men in Blue may have won the last five T20I meetings between the two sides, but a deeper look at the numbers shows this battle is far more evenly matched than the rivalry ledger alone suggests.

It's showtime - Hello, everyone! Ever since the fixtures were announced, the immediate questions were, are India and Pakistan in the same group, and if so, when is the marquee clash? It did not take long for this blockbuster to be highlighted on calendars around the world. After what has felt like an endless wait, and after all the uncertainty surrounding the game, we are here. India versus Pakistan on a Sunday. What more could you ask for?
... MATCH DAY ...

Sunday blockbuster - After all the uncertainty over whether the fixture would go ahead, decks have finally been cleared as arch-rivals India and Pakistan prepare to square off at the R Premadasa Stadium in Colombo. These two sides do not engage in bilateral cricket, which only intensifies the anticipation whenever they meet in ICC tournaments or the Asia Cup. Both teams are part of Group A, and the stakes are significant. The winner will seal progression to the Super 8 stage. For the loser, it will not be the end of their campaign, but qualification would then hinge on winning their final group game. Pakistan's journey so far - Salman Agha's men are based in Colombo for the group stage, though their first two matches were played at the city's other venue, the Sinhalese Sports Club Ground. They survived a massive scare against the Netherlands before brushing aside the USA. Middle overs a concern - A recurring theme in their two games so far, and in the lead-up to the World Cup, has been a dip in scoring rate outside the Powerplay. They have not fully capitalised on the strong starts provided by their openers and will need to address that if they are to make a deep run. Top order in focus - The last time Pakistan faced India, Sahibzada Farhan's 57 set the tone in the Asia Cup final. He, alongside Saim Ayub, will once again be crucial at the top. In the lead-up to the World Cup, Salman Agha promoted himself to number three to counter spin outside the Powerplay, but is yet to make a significant impact. Babar Azam has found runs, yet the overall tempo through the middle overs continues to invite scrutiny. Conditions versus combinations - Head coach Mike Hesson and skipper Salman Agha read the conditions well against the USA. They went in with just one specialist quick in Shaheen Afridi and loaded the side with spin options, a move that paid off handsomely. Once again, much will depend on how they assess the surface and balance their attack accordingly. There is, however, a lingering concern around Afridi's effectiveness with the new ball, as he has not been as incisive in the Powerplay as he once was. Against an Indian side that comes hard in the Powerplay and bats deep, the new ball battle could well shape the contest. India's tale - The opening two games have shown the two-time champions and reigning holders that defending the title will not be straightforward. They were reduced to 77/6 by the USA and then, against Namibia, lost their way after racing out of the blocks and failed to finish strongly. Suryakumar Yadav's side has looked less comfortable on pitches where the ball has stopped in the surface, something that could once again come into play in Colombo. Availability concerns and a tricky matchup - Abhishek Sharma missed the previous game due to a stomach infection that required hospitalisation. Although he has been discharged, he may need another match to fully recover. If Abhishek is unavailable, Sanju Samson could get another opportunity, though he has too often thrown away promising starts rather tamely. India were unsettled by Namibia's skipper, Gerhard Erasmus and his varied release points, and a similar examination awaits in Usman Tariq, whom they will be facing for the first time. His pause at release has troubled batters not only in this tournament but also in the competitions leading up to the global event, whether at the international or franchise level. The Kuldeep conundrum - The last time these sides met in Colombo during the 2023 Asia Cup in the ODI format, Kuldeep Yadav claimed a five-wicket haul. He has not featured so far this World Cup, with India preferring Axar Patel and Varun Chakaravarthy as the frontline spin options. With spinners enjoying success at the venue, the Indian think tank could be tempted to bring in the left-arm wrist spinner. The dilemma would be whether to do so at the expense of Arshdeep Singh, with Hardik Pandya and Jasprit Bumrah continuing as the primary pace options, or to trim batting depth to accommodate an extra specialist spinner. Form (Last 5 completed T20Is, most recent first) - India - WWWLW | Pakistan - WWWWW. What do the numbers say? India hold a commanding lead in the T20 World Cups. The head-to-head record stands at 7-1 in India's favour, with Pakistan's only win coming in Dubai in 2021 in a dominant 10-wicket triumph. That remains Pakistan's sole victory over their arch-rivals in Men's World Cup history, across both ODI and T20I formats. Recent form also favours India. The last five T20Is between the two sides have all gone the way of the team in blue. Spin to win? In the 6 competitive white-ball games played at the R Premadasa Stadium since the start of the year, 51 out of the 83 wickets have fallen to spin. The spinners have operated at an economy rate of 5.66. In comparison, the pacers have claimed 32 wickets at a higher economy rate of 7.28, underlining the influence spin has had at the venue. Weather check - Sri Lanka's Department of Meteorology has flagged the possibility of a developing low-pressure system in the region. Typically, in these parts, the heat builds through the day before the heavens open in the evening. Let's hope that is not the case this time and that we get an uninterrupted spectacle under the lights.
